extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students and general readers of combinatorics and discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and proof-templates for classical combinatorial theorems (Sperner, Erdős–Ko–Rado, Hall, de Bruijn, Dehn, Sperner's lemma, coupon-collector, birthday paradox) and illustrative proof techniques (double counting, parity, coloring, spectral methods). Useful for learning, reproducing, or teaching combinatorial proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of the projective-plane graph G_p (vertex/degree/edge counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the graph G_p built from one-dimensional subspaces of a 3-dim vector space over F_p: number of vertices n = p^2 + p + 1; each two vertices have a unique common neighbor; every one-dimensional subspace corresponds to a vertex; degrees are p or p+1 depending on whether the representative lies on the conic x^2+y^2+z^2=0; there are p+1 vertices of degree p and p^2 vertices of degree p+1; explicit formula for |E| derived (expressed in terms of p or n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive counts by double counting and linear algebra: count nonzero vectors, divide by p−1 to get one-dimensional subspaces; adjacency determined by solutions of a linear equation (a two-dimensional solution space gives p+1 solutions unless the vector is self-orthogonal). Use the trace/eigenvalue trick on the symmetric adjacency-like matrix A (with a_ij = 1 iff <v_i,v_j>=0) and analyze A^2 = p I + J to obtain trace(A) = p+1; this yields the count of self-orthogonal vectors (vertices of degree p).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sperner's Lemma (planar triangulation form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a triangulation of a triangle with vertex-colors from {1,2,3} satisfying: each big vertex V_i is colored i, vertices along edge V_iV_j get only colors i or j, interior vertices arbitrary. Then there exists a small triangle whose three vertices have all three different colors. Moreover, the number of such tricolored small triangles is odd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via a partial dual graph: include only dual edges crossing edges colored 1 and 2; degrees of dual vertices correspond to whether the primal small triangle is tricolored (degree 1) or contains colors 1 and 2 (degree 2). The outside dual vertex has odd degree because along the big edge V1V2 there is an odd number of alternations between colors 1 and 2; parity of odd-degree vertices (even number) then forces an odd number of tricolored inner triangles. This lemma is the combinatorial engine for Brouwer's fixed point argument via increasingly fine triangulations and a limiting argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem (n=2 consequence via Sperner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every continuous function f : B^n → B^n has a fixed point (presented here for n=2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to simplex Δ (2-simplex). For an arbitrarily fine sequence of triangulations T_k (mesh→0), color each vertex v by λ(v):=min{i : f(v)_i < v_i} under the assumption f has no fixed point. This coloring satisfies Sperner's boundary conditions, so each triangulation contains a tricolored small triangle. Extract a convergent subsequence of vertices and use continuity to show the limit point v satisfies f(v)=v, contradiction. The exposition includes construction of triangulations (e.g., barycentric subdivisions) and the limiting argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: de Bruijn's theorem on rectangular tilings (integer side criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rectangle is tiled by rectangles all of which have at least one side of integer length, then the tiled rectangle has at least one side of integer length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three proofs highlighted: (1) analytic/trigonometric integral proof: integrate e^{2πi(x+y)} over rectangles; a one-dimensional integral vanishes iff the side length difference is integer, use additivity over the tiling; (2) checkerboard coloring with 1/2 × 1/2 squares: each small rectangle has equal black and white area, forcing the big rectangle to have equal black/white only when it has integer side; (3) parity graph argument: form bipartite graph between integer-coordinate corners and tiles, count incident edges parity to force another integer corner on boundary. These present alternative proof techniques (Fourier/integral, coloring, parity/double-counting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dehn's theorem on tiling rectangles by squares (rational ratio criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rectangle can be tiled with squares if and only if the ratio of its side lengths is a rational number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses a linear-algebraic 'Dehn invariant' style argument: scale so rectangle is a × 1 with a irrational, extend the set of appearing side lengths to a Q-vector-space V(A) with basis containing 1 and a, define a linear functional f with f(1)=1, f(a)=-1 and zero on other basis elements; extend f linearly and define 'area' as product f(c)f(d) for side lengths c,d in V(A). Compute area(R)=f(a)f(1)=-1, while every square contributes nonnegative area f(t)^2≥0, contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sperner's Theorem (antichain size)
rubrics_metrics.description: The maximum size of an antichain of subsets of an n-set is binomial(n, floor(n/2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lubell's short proof: count all chains ∅=C_0⊂C_1⊂...⊂C_n (there are n! chains). For each A∈F of size k, exactly k!(n−k)! chains contain A. Since chains contain at most one member of an antichain, summing k!(n−k)! over members of F ≤ n!. Dividing by n! and replacing denominators by the maximum binomial coefficient yields |F| ≤ max_k binom(n,k) = binom(n, floor(n/2)). The extremal families are all k-sets for k = floor(n/2) (or the two central layers when n is odd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Erdős–Ko–Rado Theorem (intersecting k-families)
rubrics_metrics.description: For n ≥ 2k, the maximum size of an intersecting family of k-subsets of an n-set is binomial(n−1, k−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Katona's elegant proof via circular permutations: consider cyclic orderings of the n elements around a circle; an arc of length k is k consecutive elements. Lemma: if n ≥ 2k and t distinct arcs pairwise intersect in an edge then t ≤ k. For any cyclic permutation, at most k sets from an intersecting family appear as consecutive k-blocks; count over all (n−1)! cyclic permutations and divide by how many permutations represent a fixed set (k!(n−k)!) to obtain |F| ≤ k(n−1)! / (k!(n−k)!) = binom(n−1,k−1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hall's Marriage Theorem (system of distinct representatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection A1,...,An of subsets of a finite set X has a system of distinct representatives (SDR) iff for every m (1≤m≤n) the union of any m of the Ai contains at least m elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction with case-splitting on existence of a 'critical family' (a subcollection of size r<n whose union has exactly r elements). In the non-critical case choose an element x in A_n, remove it and apply induction; in the critical-case construct an SDR for the critical subfamily and apply induction to the remaining sets after removing the critical union. The theorem is presented with the standard combinatorial interpretation ('marriage theorem') and remarks on extensions (k SDRs when each Ai has size k and no element lies in more than k sets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Birthday paradox (distinct birthdays probability estimate)
rubrics_metrics.description: For n people (assume 365 equally likely birthdays) the probability that all have different birthdays is p(n) = ∏_{i=1}^{n-1} (1 - i/365). Numerical facts: p(n)<1/2 already at n=23; it drops below 9% at n=42; this probability is zero for n>365 by the pigeonhole principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive p(n) by sequential conditioning: the i+1-th person avoids the previous i birthdays with probability 1 − i/365. The formula generalizes to balls-into-boxes: p(n,K)=∏_{i=1}^{n-1}(1 − i/K). Use approximations (e.g., exponentials) for estimates when n is moderate relative to K.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coupon-collector expected time and tail bound
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are n distinct coupons sampled uniformly with replacement, the expected number of draws to collect all coupons is n H_n ≈ n log n. Moreover, if V_n denotes the time to collect all n, then for m = n log n + c n, Prob(V_n > m) ≤ e^{−c}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute expected waiting time in successive phases: if k distinct coupons collected, expected draws to next new coupon is 1/(1−k/n). Summing k from 0 to n−1 yields n H_n. Tail bound via union bound + geometric/probabilistic estimate: Prob(some coupon missing after m draws) ≤ n (1 − 1/n)^m < n e^{-m/n} ≤ e^{-c} for m = n log n + c n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-technique rubric: double counting, parity, coloring, and spectral methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The chapter emphasizes several high-level combinatorial proof techniques: double counting/pigeonhole arguments, parity/graph-degree counting, coloring arguments (checkerboard and Sperner-type colorings), analytic/integral methods (Fourier-type integrals), and linear-algebraic spectral arguments (analyzing eigenvalues / trace of symmetric matrices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: double counting to obtain cardinalities and bounds (chains/antichains, edges in bipartite graph for tilings); parity arguments for counting odd-degree vertices (Sperner's lemma dual-graph, tiling corner parity); coloring to force contradictions (checkerboard for de Bruijn proof, Sperner boundary-coloring); spectral trick: form adjacency-like matrix A with entries 1 when vectors are orthogonal and use A^2 = pI + J to deduce eigenvalue multiplicities and trace consequences. Use each technique where it naturally simplifies combinatorial counting or existence proofs; many proofs shown are short 'proofs from the book' illustrating elegance and minimal machinery.
